opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, so a big part of it comes down to how naturally Transformers handle the kind of masking we do in V-JEPA. The way we set it up, we take a video, break it into spatiotemporal patches, these little tubelets that span a few frames and a small spatial region, and then we mask out large chunks of that video. The context encoder only sees the visible patches, and a predictor has to fill in the representations of the missing regions.

With a Transformer, the input is just a set of tokens. You don't need a dense grid the way you would with a convolutional network. So you can simply drop the masked tokens and only process the ones that are visible. That's very convenient, and it's also a huge efficiency win. With video, the number of tokens gets large quickly, and if you're masking something like ninety percent of the clip, you're only paying compute for a small fraction of it.

On the predictor side, it's similarly natural. You feed in the encoded context tokens along with learnable mask tokens that carry positional embeddings, and those tell the predictor where in space and time it's supposed to make a prediction. Attention then lets every mask token look at all of the context and pull in whatever's relevant, whether that's something nearby in the same frame or something several frames earlier. That global, content-dependent mixing is exactly what you want when you're trying to reason about what's happening in an occluded part of a scene over time.

There's also a practical side. Vision Transformers scale very well, there's a mature ecosystem of training recipes, and you get a standard backbone that people can drop into downstream tasks. So it wasn't that the JEPA idea strictly requires a Transformer. The objective is architecture-agnostic in principle. But the tokenized, set-based view of the input lines up really cleanly with predicting in representation space from partial observations, and that made it the obvious choice for us.

r001.rationale: The response says the JEPA objective is architecture-agnostic, but it does not state that JEPA’s input and target signals need not be defined by masking parts of a video.

r002.rationale: It explicitly says the Transformer can drop masked tokens and process only visible ones, saving compute when most of a video is masked.

r003.rationale: The response discusses positional embeddings and global attention, but does not state that Transformers lack an intrinsic representation of spatiotemporal distance between tokens.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so I think the key thing to understand about V-JEPA is that it's fundamentally a prediction task in representation space. We take a video, we mask out large chunks of it, spatially and temporally, and we ask the model to predict the representations of those missing regions from the parts it can see. And the important part is that it's not predicting pixels, it's predicting abstract features produced by a target encoder. So the architecture has to be good at a few very specific things, and Transformers happen to be good at exactly those things.

The first is flexibility with respect to the input. Because we're masking, the encoder only ever sees a subset of the video. With a convolutional network, the inductive bias is tied to a regular grid, and when you remove a big block of the grid, you either have to fill it in with something or you end up with the network leaking information about where the holes are. With a Vision Transformer you just drop the tokens. You tokenize the video into spatiotemporal patches, you keep the visible ones, you throw away the masked ones, and the model never even sees them. That's really clean, and it's also computationally efficient, because you're only running the encoder on the visible portion.

The second is the predictor. In JEPA, we have this separate narrow network whose job is to take the context representations plus positional information about what you want to predict, and produce the predicted representations. A Transformer is a very natural fit there because you can just feed in learnable mask tokens that carry the positional embedding of the target patches, let them attend to the context, and read out the prediction. There's no fixed spatial layout you need to respect. You can ask for any region, at any time step, and the mechanism is the same.

And then the third thing, which I think people underappreciate, is that attention gives you long-range dependencies across both space and time for free. For video, a lot of what you want the model to learn is how things move, how objects persist, how one part of a scene relates to another part a second later. Convolutions build that up slowly, layer by layer, through local receptive fields. Attention lets every patch talk to every other patch from the first layer. For a task that's about predicting what's happening in a part of the video you can't see, based on what's happening elsewhere, that global view matters a lot.

There's also just a practical point, which is that Transformers scale really well with data and compute, and they've become something like a lingua franca across modalities. So when we think about JEPA as a general recipe, not just for video but as a way of learning world models from any kind of sensory input, having a backbone that's largely modality-agnostic is a big advantage. We're not designing a new architecture for every signal. We're designing a learning objective, and the Transformer is the substrate that lets us focus on that.

r001.rationale: The response describes masking video regions in V-JEPA and says the broader JEPA recipe can apply to other sensory inputs. It does not state that JEPA’s input and target signals need not be defined by masking video parts.

r002.rationale: It says the Vision Transformer drops masked tokens and runs the encoder only on the visible portion, making the approach computationally efficient.

r003.rationale: The response says the predictor has no fixed spatial layout to respect, but does not clearly state that Transformers have no intrinsic representation of spatiotemporal distance between video tokens.

astra-6.text:
I think the key property is that Transformers let us operate on a set of tokens without requiring a fixed grid of inputs. That’s a really natural fit for the masking approach in V-JEPA. We divide a video into patches, mask out some of those patches, and ask the model to predict representations of the missing regions from the context it can see.

With a Transformer, we can feed only the visible patches into the encoder. Positional information tells the model where those patches came from in space and time, and attention lets it gather information across the video. Then the predictor uses those contextual representations, together with the positions of the missing patches, to predict their representations.

So there’s a nice alignment between the architecture and the learning task. We can use different masking patterns, process the visible context efficiently, and learn relationships across space and time within the same architecture.

r001.rationale: The response describes masking video patches as central to V-JEPA’s task; it does not state that input and target signals need not be defined by masking.

r002.rationale: It says the Transformer encoder receives only visible patches and that this lets the model process visible context efficiently.

r003.rationale: It discusses positional information for locating patches, but does not state that Transformers lack an intrinsic representation of spatiotemporal distance.

sol-6.1.text:
Yeah, so a big part of V-JEPA is predicting representations of missing parts of a video from the parts that you can see. Transformers are a very natural fit for that because they operate on tokens. We can divide a video into these little space-time patches, turn them into tokens, and then choose which tokens we give to the encoder and which ones we ask the predictor to predict.

And with attention, the model can bring together information from different spatial locations and different points in time. If something is hidden in one frame, there might be useful information about it in another frame. The architecture gives the model a flexible way to use that context, without us having to specify exactly which relationships it should look for.

r001.rationale: It describes predicting missing video parts from visible parts, but does not say JEPA inputs and targets need not be defined by video masking.

r002.rationale: It says tokens are selected for the encoder and predictor, but does not explain that processing only unmasked tokens makes masking computationally efficient.

r003.rationale: It describes attention across locations and time, but does not state that Transformers lack an intrinsic representation of spatiotemporal distance.
